description: CSE undergraduate interested in software development, web development, and hackathons. Participating independently in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
summary: Mission Bench is a browser-based game where players design and launch a complete space mission. Players choose a mission objective (Earth observation, lunar science or a deep space telescope), a launch vehicle, an orbit, scientific instruments, solar panels and a communications antenna. A live dashboard shows mass, power, budget and data limits, so every decision has a visible consequence. When players launch, the game checks launcher and orbit compatibility, simulates power and data flow, applies a random event such as a solar flare or antenna glitch, and produces a score with a report explaining why the mission succeeded or failed. Roles for a team of up to four players (Mission Planner, Resource Manager, Science Lead, Spacecraft Engineer) are built into the interface. It helps beginners understand the trade-offs in real mission design.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Mission Bench lets players experience the chain of space mission design in a few minutes. Players pick an objective, launch vehicle, orbit, instruments, solar panels and antenna. A dashboard tracks mass, power, budget and data live. Launching runs a simulation that checks whether the rocket can reach the orbit and lift the spacecraft, whether power covers all systems, and whether the antenna can send home the data the instruments produce. A random event (solar flare or antenna glitch) tests the design, and keeping a 25% margin protects the mission. The game ends with a score out of 100 and a report explaining each success or failure in plain language.

HOW IT ADDRESSES THE CHALLENGE

- Objective-first design: the objective decides which orbits and instruments are useful.

- Every decision has a consequence: more instruments raise science value but also mass, power, cost and data.

- No single perfect solution: different combinations of rocket, orbit and instruments can succeed.

- Launcher and orbit compatibility and mass checks are built in.

- Team roles for up to four players (Mission Planner, Resource Manager, Science Lead, Spacecraft Engineer).

- Educational: short explanations teach orbit, payload capacity, power and data rate, and the report explains why a mission worked or failed.

IMPACT

Students rarely get to experiment with a whole mission. The game makes system-level trade-offs concrete and encourages redesign and relaunch.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with no external libraries. It works on desktop and mobile, with light and dark themes. All values are simplified teaching numbers, not real mission data. The structure is inspired by NASA's mission segments and the trade-study approach of NASA's Mission Design Lab.

FUTURE WORK

Online multiplayer, more scenarios and difficulty levels, an orbit visualisation, and leaderboards.

AI DISCLOSURE

Code and text were written with help from Claude (an AI assistant by Anthropic) and reviewed and tested by our team.
